event: Internet services and phone lines were cut off by the military council across all 18 townships of Kachin State at 10:00am local time on Jul. 21. People resorted to using Chinese providers by the border when possible, or Starlink if they had it available in their area. By Aug. 20, some mobile connections started to be restored in parts of Kachin. Myitkyina was still cutoff as of Sep. 13 as locals tried to connect with IP Star and Starlink. However, the regime was inspecting local businesses for satellite connection nodes and making arrests in the process. The shutdown was still prevalent across Kachin State as of Oct. 3 and Nov. 18. Connections were restored on Mytel in Bhamo around 4:00pm (local time) on Dec. 2. Myitkyina regained partial access to MPT service by Jan. 6, 2025, and some other townships (like Danai City) had MPT, Ooredoo, and Atom service in certain neighborhoods, but most of Kachin State had been undergoing a shutdown for 6 months as of Jan. 21, 2025 as fighting was ongoing between the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and junta. By Jun. 17, 2025, Mytel mobile service returned to Myitkyina. As of Jun. 25, 2025, the following townships had service available: Myitkyina (Mytel, Atom), Hpakant (MPT), Puta-O (Ooredoo, Atom), Khaung Lan Phu (MEC), and Naungmon town had some MPT, with the rest Kachin state offline. The state reached one-year of a shutdown on Jul. 21, 2025. Mohnyin had Mytel mobile service return on Sep. 9, 2025. The state reached 15 months of a shutdown on Oct. 21, 2025. Puta-O had Mytel service return by Oct. 28, 2025. The state reached 16 months of a shutdown by late Nov. 2025.

event: TikTok and other ByteDance apps were blocked in the US from 22:30 (UTC-5, US Eastern Standard Time) on Jan. 18 until 12:30 (UTC-5, US Eastern Standard Time) on Jan. 19. Ahead of a mandated ban on Jan. 19 as upheld by the US Supreme Court due to the lack of a sale of TikTok to US ownership, TikTok disabled the service and major providers like Apple and Google removed all relevant apps from their app stores in compliance. President-elect Trump indicated he would grant an extension to TikTok's required sale, causing the block to be lifted. Normal traffic did not fully return on TikTok until at least Jan. 22, and the app didn't return to the Apple app store until Feb. 13, meaning only users who had existing downloads of the app could use it. The app is still legally under a de jure nationwide ban as of Dec. 2025, but the Trump administration has repeatedly halted enforcement of the ban as they negotiate with the Chinese over the app's ownership with US investors. This is the first shutdown recorded for the US.

event: Alongside the full network shutdown between Oct. 29 and Nov. 3, authorities in Tanzania imposed multiple platform blocks in the lead-up to and following Election Day, targeting apps that weren't already blocked under existing orders (Grindr, Clubhouse, X, and Telegram). According to OONI data, WhatsApp was blocked from Oct. 29 to Nov. 6, Signal was blocked from Oct. 28 to Nov. 4, FB Messenger was blocked between Nov. 3 and Nov. 4. TikTok was blocked Oct. 28 and still remains inaccessible. The blocks were initially applied inconsistently across providers, and only the ongoing block of TikTok seems to be uniformly applied after Nov. 3 as evident by nearly 100% of OONI measurements returning as anomalies per day. Similar to the full network shutdown, these blocks coincided with mass killings of protestors and serious human rights abuses by Tanzanian authorities, and the one that remained in effect in early December was likely continued in anticipation of Dec. 9 protests. The TikTok blocking finally ended by Dec. 29.

telcos_involved: Iran: MCI (TCI), Iran: MTN Irancell, Iran: Rightel (Tamin Telecom), Iran: Shatel
event: Beginning Dec. 29, Iranian authorities imposed hyper-localized disruptions and throttling in areas of Bushehr, Ilam, Isfahan, Fasa, Mashhad, Sanandaj, Shiraz, and Tehran where anti-regime protests were quickly expanding. These shutdowns affected primarily mobile networks, with fiber connections also degraded in places like Isfahan, with service unusable for either some or all of the day, and with access limited to just the domestic intranet. In this period, security forces began their crackdown on largely peaceful protesters with unlawful use of force and firearms, as well as mass arbitrary arrests, which resulted in the killing of at least 28 protesters and bystanders, including children, in 8 provinces beginning Dec. 31.
